lesson.title: The Trap Named
lesson.subtitle: mon frère / ma sœur, son frère ('his OR her brother'), and mon before feminine vowels (mon opinion).

hook.title: Why 'Her Brother' Is son frère and 'My Opinion' Is mon opinion
hook.content: Trap 1: son/sa/ses agrees with the thing owned, never the owner — so 'her brother' is son frère (masculine!) and 'his sister' is sa sœur (feminine!). Trap 2: Before ANY feminine noun starting with a vowel or mute H (opinion, histoire, université, amie), ma/ta/sa switch to mon/ton/son to prevent a vowel crash: mon opinion, ton histoire, son amie!

footnotes.title: How liaison makes mon opinion sound smooth
footnotes.content: In mon‿opinion (/mɔ̃.nɔ.pi.njɔ̃/), the final /n/ of mon jumps onto opinion as a clean consonant bridge!

pattern.title: Ignore the Owner's Gender, and Use mon/ton/son Before ANY Vowel
pattern.content: Check the word right after the possessive for vowel/mute-H first, then gender.
pattern.linguist_note: Prevocalic feminine mon/ton/son avoids hiatus before vowel-initial feminine nouns.
pattern.trap_note: Never write *ma amie, *ma opinion, or *sa histoire — vowel-initial feminine nouns ALWAYS take mon, ton, son!

exercises.prompt: Match each English phrase with its correct French possessive:
exercises.target_answer: son frère, sa sœur, mon opinion, ton histoire, sa maison
exercises.meaning: her brother (frère is masculine!), his sister (sœur is feminine!), my opinion (feminine, starts with vowel!), your story (feminine, mute H!), his / her house (maison is feminine)
exercises.explanation: Look only at the noun owned — and use mon/ton/son before any vowel or mute H.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'my female friend' (amie, feminine starting with a vowel)?
exercises.explanation: Before a vowel, ma switches to mon: mon amie!

exercises.prompt: Paul is talking about his mother (la mère), and Marie is talking about her father (le père). Which pair is right?
exercises.meaning: his mother (sa mère) / her father (son père)
exercises.explanation: mère is feminine (sa mère); père is masculine (son père).

exercises.idea: it is my opinion and it is her story
cues: It is my opinion → C'est mon opinion
and it is her story → et c'est son histoire
idea_parts: second clause → et c'est son histoire
exercises.target_answer: C'est mon opinion et c'est son histoire
exercises.meaning: It is my opinion and it is her story
exercises.explanation: Both opinion and histoire take mon/son because they start with a vowel/mute H!

diagnosis.cue: Use mon opinion and son histoire.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Elle cherche son frère et son père
exercises.target_answer: Elle cherche son frère et son père
exercises.meaning: She is looking for her brother and her father
exercises.explanation: Both frère and père are masculine, so 'her' is son for both.
exercises.affirmation: You kept son before both masculine nouns!

summary.outcome: Master son/sa agreement with the possessed noun and mon/ton/son before vowel-initial feminine nouns.

use_example.german: C'est mon idée, mon opinion et mon histoire.
use_example.english: It is my idea, my opinion, and my story.

summary.takeaway: Ignore the owner's gender, and use mon/ton/son before every vowel.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([1402] Famille Gym): see how The Trap Named leads directly into Famille Gym.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "It is my opinion and it is her story" in French:
twist.target_answer: C'est mon opinion et c'est son histoire
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "C'est mon opinion et c'est son histoire" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of The Trap Named.

mon.context_phrase: C'est mon père et mon amie.
mon.context_translation: It's my father and my (female) friend.
mon.etymology_derivation: Also steps in before feminine nouns starting with a vowel (mon opinion, mon idée) to avoid a vowel clash!

ma.etymology_derivation: Used before feminine singular nouns starting with a consonant.

mes.etymology_derivation: One plural form for both genders.

son.shift_rule: Agrees with the thing owned, NOT the owner
son.context_translation: Marie is looking for her brother.
son.etymology_derivation: The biggest English-transfer trap: son frère can mean 'his brother' OR 'her brother' because frère is masculine!

sa.shift_rule: Agrees with the thing owned, NOT the owner
sa.etymology_derivation: Paul is male, but maison is feminine, so it MUST be sa maison!

père.etymology_derivation: Latin pater — the root of paternal, patriarch. English kept the root, French kept the word.

frère.etymology_derivation: Latin frāter — fraternal, friar (the brother of the church).

sœur.etymology_derivation: Latin soror — English kept the Latin sisterhood in sorority.

opinion.etymology_derivation: Latin opinio 'what one supposes'. Starts with a vowel, so la loses its a: l'opinion.

histoire.etymology_derivation: One French word covers both 'history' and 'story'.

ami.etymology_derivation: In liaison, un ami sounds like /œ̃.na.mi/ and mes amis like /me.za.mi/.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
